CB MAD TRUST 2021

By: Sasha Schwendenwein | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
What have we built and where are we going? A revamp of the trust will show what it has done for the South African children and those its helped

Unique Selling Point:
We are speaking with children who benefitted from the trust - the doctors and nurses are compiling this list. We will see a child from 5 years ago who had burns and what they look like today as an example etc

THEN we are speaking to the Doctors and nurses from the hospitals who can tell us how the trust has helped them keep patients alive.

We are speaking to business owners (this is new) who benefitted from the local community in building the new sebokeng wing.

We have already interviewed Donors, and asked why they chose the trust and how it it has changed them.

We are 20 projects in and have helped countless children in South Africa, but we have also made the mothers and fathers feel safe in the knowledge that their child is getting the best care. We have also raised over R145 million! And in this, allowed nurses and doctors to know they have the equipment they need to save a life. This is an extraordinary project and needs to be told and shown differently than before.

We are actually go into the lives of those we have helped.

We will also interview doctors who we have educated and sent overseas and who are now back and saving lives here! This isn't going to be about ribbon cutting but rather about showing and not telling our audience the difference its made.



Summary:
A Brief History
In the decade since the launch of the Carte Blanche ‘Making a Difference’ campaign, over R145-million has been raised to equip and renovate Paediatric Operating Theatres, ICUs and High Care Wards in 10 State academic hospitals in six of South Africa’s nine provinces. Each of the Trust’s projects have had the benefited from the expertise of some of the country’s top specialists in the fields of hospital development, architecture and clinical, electrical and mechanical engineering. Thousands of hours have been contributed for the benefit of each project’s success. In turn, this has resulted in long-term benefits to thousands of children in State hospitals throughout South Africa.

The Carte Blanche “Making a Difference” Trust has commenced its 19th project, namely to create a new Paediatric Unit at Ngwelezana Hospital in KZN’s Umhlathuze Municipality. The upliftment of paediatric services for trauma, burns and orthopedic at the hospital will be addressed by way of overhauling a building that has been earmarked for this purpose and equipping it with appropriate equipment. In addition to the work in various hospitals, the trust has completed several projects in aftercare centres and orphanages, as well as initiating and securing the funding for feeding programmes for our child welfare beneficiaries in Gauteng, the North West province and KwaZulu-Natal.

Further information:
Sebokeng Hospital Paediatric Lower High Care Unit Project



Interviews Friday 17 September 2021;



Dr Theletsane: HOD Paediatrics: Intwerview at 11H00

What was the impact of the 2016 Infant High Care Unit Project on him, his staff and the children (currently undergoing rejuvenation)?

What are the details of the new project, under construction - the Paeds Lower High Care Unit that, in his view, have significance on his and his teams wherewithal to deliver class care to the young of Sebokeng? How does this impact on him personally as a doctor?

How did he provide personal input into planning & design of the new Unit? Has this been implemented practically?



Acting Unit Manager: Nursing Sister Matieho Namani: Interview at 11H15

Similar questions as those posed to Dr Theletsane

Dr Mashele: Sebokeng Hospital Clinical Manager: 11H30
How long has Dr worked at the Hospital?

Dr Mashele is a closely involved member of team on building projects at the hospital – what is his view of the developments of Phase 1 & 2 and what bearing does this have on his Clinical Management of the hospital? What bearing do these projects have on the delivery of healthcare to the children of the Sedibeng community?

Interviews:



Billy Neethling: Jomarel Construction Principal and Foreman: Roland Marsh 11H45



July 2021 saw some of the worst acts of destruction and looting in decades in SA.



This period intersected at the heart of the construction programme of our Paediatric Lower High Care Unit Project at Sebokeng Hospital.



Thanks to the commitment of our contractors and local business owners and labourers, only one day of construction time was lost.



From the community (remembering that these local companies employ a lot of locals who built the project)



Sejako: Local lady business owner of ISS Plumbing: (plumbing on the project) 12H00



John: Local business owner of ATL Lupula Electrical (electricians for the project) 12H15



Jacob and John: local previously unemployed workmen from Sebokeng who worked on construction from start to end of project

Background:

The creation and equipping of the 6 bed Infant High Care Ward at Sebokeng Hospital, sponsored by South 32, has reference. In a period calculated as 21 months between September 2016 to May 2018: 348 infants have been assisted. The High Care Unit now attends to approximately 20 Infants per month each of whom has an average stay of roughly 3 days. Approximately 1/3 of the Ward 3 bungalow was used to create the High Care Ward, with the balance of 2/3rds of the space lying disconnected from services and unutilised.

Sebokeng Hospital is a peri urban regional, level 2 hospital. Referrals arise from all the primary health care facilities in the Vaal from as well as from various Level 1 district hospitals including Kopanong. Sebokeng Hospital is servicing a burgeoning population of both formal and informal settlements in the Sedibeng District. The increased population and growth in burden of disease leaves Sebokeng in a position where it faces a shortage of bed capacity and critical infrastructural resources in meeting the needs of its community. As part of the endemic shortage of nurses and doctors in South Africa, Sebokeng Hospital also faces these critical staff shortages. The issue has been addressed with regards to doctors in the Infant High Care Ward, by way of agreements reached with Chris Hani Bara which sends two paediatric registrars to staff the NICU & Infant HCW. These positions are sponsored by Sebokeng Hospital which makes this training programme possible.

Statement of need:

All patients who arrive at Sebokeng Hospital are admitted via the Casualty Unit at the hospital – irrespective whether or not these patients be recently discharged neonates and children – or adults.The waiting time for babies is no different to adults and infants are assessed by people who are used to adults.The Nurses are operating at 25% of what is needed in terms of patient numbers and are not specialised in Neonatology or Paediatrics.

There is capacity for 36 Neonates in the NICU, but even with the Infant High Care Ward in place, the NICU typically holds 42 – 56 neonates at any time. Infants should never ever be readmitted to the NICU, but diverted immediately to an Infant Facility in order to effect adequate infection control. Oftentimes there is only 1 ICU nurse to 6- 7 patients. This critical nurse shortage has impact on outcomes. Mortality of infants and children has actually increased in the General Casualty Admissions Ward. Due to the constraints of bed space, older children are also being admitted to the Infant High Care Unit – placing an additional restraint of capacity on these services.

The Carte Blanche Making a Difference Trust seeks to address growing mortality by proposing to renovate the balance of 2/3rds of Ward 3 alongside the Infant High Care Unit. The greatest need is to create expanded neonatal & Infant High Care Capacity for children who are readmitted to the Hospital, and who should be quarantined.

Apart from repairs need to the entire Ward 3 Bungalow roof including new sheeting and sealing, the 1st step would be to get medical gases and oxygen services back into the middle section of Ward 3, adjacent to the Infant High Care Ward. If left to the DOH, they would only replace pipes and points – not pendants to bring in the necessary services, nor extraction.

In addition, The Carte Blanche Trust seeks to refurbish the 1st part of the Ward 3 bungalow into a dedicated Neonatal & Paediatric Casualty Admissions Ward. This would ensure that children are

admitted/readmitted and diverted to the appropriate ward within a timeframe that prevents their deterioration, making them ineligible for treatment. Babies that are readmitted to Sebokeng Hospital would be separated permanently from their younger, more vulnerable peers. The Dedicated Neonatal & Casualty Ward should ideally cater for a walk in triage point centre with seating available, and 7 beds with 1 isolated overnight room (if contagions are suspected) in the back.

Script:


These Community Members Are Here Plumbing, Tiling, Painting And Together Building Something Extraordinary… a high care children’s ward in the impoverished community of Sebokeng BUILT BY DONORS OF THE CARTE BLANCHE TRUST.

LINK: PROJECTS LIKE WARD 3 AT SEBOKENG HOSPITAL HAVE BECOME GEMS TO THE LOCAL COMMUNITY, THIS IS BECAUSE IMPORTANTLY THE COMMUNITY ALSO HELPED BUILD THEM.

Some of those contractors are plumber, Sejako Netshivhale, builder, Mhlanganisi Nzula, and Painter, and Leo Mramba who's expecting to become a first time father.



Leo: Right now, I can bring my own girlfriend because she's going to get a baby. I'm very happy to come into work here and doing what I'm doing for babies and mamas also.

Sejako: this is my first project this year because of COVID. You know, things were a little bit difficult. Women musn’t be afraid to do this kind of a job, thinking maybe it's a men's world, you know, luckily, women can also do it.

For a person knowing that they are part of something, they tend to care more about it, get involved knowing that, uh, if this place is not working, that means our children or the people in the community will not get assistance.

ENTER THE CARTE BLANCHE MAKING A DIFFERENCE TRUST AND ITS COLLABORATORS. TRAVELLING THE LENGTH AND BREADTH OF THE COUNTRY FOR THE LAST 13 YEARS, KEY AREAS OF NEED WERE IDENTIFIED AND UNIQUE CHILDREN’S CRITICAL CARE FACILITIES PUT IN PLACE.

In 2016 the Trust chose Sebokeng hospital to build a 6 bed Infant High Care Ward which saw 348 infants in its first 21 months.

Dr. I knew that I could relax and just do what I learnt which is to take care of children as, opposed to being worried about, you know, will we have the machine to be able to help this child breathe?

Dr Thapelo Theletsane has worked at various public hospitals nationwide...But his journey to become the Head of Department in Pediatrics at the Sebokeng Hospital actually begins and ends with this Gauteng community.

Amazingly enough, I was actually a patient here in the 80s. even much more amazing to be back to serve our community.



LINK: IMAGINE ARRIVING AT A HOSPITAL WITH A BABY IN DISTRESS… ONLY TO BE TOLD YOU’LL NEED TO WAIT IN LINE BECAUSE THERE ARE NO BEDS OR TO BE TURNED AWAY BECAUSE THEY DO NOT HAVE INFANT WARDS… THAT IS A REALITY THAT SOME PUBLIC HOSPITALS FACE.

You need to have the love for the children. when we come in contact with very sick babies, it is heartbreaking. But as you treat the child and the child gets better, you know your heart gets warmed up.

Pushing the contractors to go beyond is Project foreman Roland Marsh

It’s something for me to feel proud of that I did something for a big community such as sebokeng that's in need of something like this here thats uplifting a bit the thing is it's like when you're going to a hospital, it's mostly a negative But when you’re here it's like it's bright. It's clear it's like you feel welcomed.

After years of planning, and despite the Covid Pandemic, THIS YEAR the Trust committed to expanding this High Care Ward by a further 8 beds to meet the demands of a growing community, which suffers from a crippling shortage of facilities and a high infant mortality rate often due to children arriving at Sebokeng as a result of malnutrition.

This project has been put together by the community for the community.

Principal builder Billy Neethling from the appointed contractor Jo-Moral believes the high community engagement numbers are extraordinary.

We have averaged probably between 63 and 65 per cent of local labor.

On top of everything the project was put in danger in July during the riots and looting which saw Sebokeng hit hard.

BN: Although the the areas, the three malls that are now off, we actually did a lot of our procuring of materials and that they were badly damaged and we we had to then source materials from elsewhere.

But again, this team triumphed, only losing a single day's work.

Projects like Sebokeng go beyond borders; this hospital services the region - a staggering million people - including absorbing patients from district hospitals like Kopanong whose acting CEO is Dr Percy Mabena.

PB: So patients must start at the clinic and then they should be sent to us if they cannot be managed, So babies of patients that we cannot manage should be sent to a regional hospital, which is this one now. So you can imagine what will happen if we can't find a bed for for that baby. bringing these now we are creating more beds for us so that we can be able to send patients to Sebokeng.

Raising a child takes a community, but in Sebokeng, this community is also taking ownership of their children’s futures.

We have averaged probably between 63 and 65 per cent of local labor. On top of everything the project was put in danger in July during the riots and looting which saw Sebokeng hit hard. BN: Although the the areas, the three malls that are now off, we actually did a lot of our procuring of materials and that they were badly damaged and we we had to then source materials from elsewhere. But again, this team triumphed, only losing a single day's work. Projects like Sebokeng go beyond borders; this hospital services the region - a staggering million people - including absorbing patients from district hospitals like Kopanong whose acting CEO is Dr Percy Mabena. PB: So patients must start at the clinic and then they should be sent to us if they cannot be managed, So babies of patients that we cannot manage should be sent to a regional hospital, which is this one now. So you can imagine what will happen if we can't find a bed for for that baby. bringing these now we are creating more beds for us so that we can be able to send patients to Sebokeng. Raising a child takes a community, but in Sebokeng, this community is also taking ownership of their children’s futures.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): What have we built and where are we going? A revamp of the trust will show what it has done for the South African children and those its helped
metadata.Unique Selling Point: We are speaking with children who benefitted from the trust - the doctors and nurses are compiling this list. We will see a child from 5 years ago who had burns and what they look like today as an example etc THEN we are speaking to the Doctors and nurses from the hospitals who can tell us how the trust has helped them keep patients alive. We are speaking to business owners (this is new) who benefitted from the local community in building the new sebokeng wing. We have already interviewed Donors, and asked why they chose the trust and how it it has changed them. We are 20 projects in and have helped countless children in South Africa, but we have also made the mothers and fathers feel safe in the knowledge that their child is getting the best care. We have also raised over R145 million! And in this, allowed nurses and doctors to know they have the equipment they need to save a life. This is an extraordinary project and needs to be told and shown differently than before. We are actually go into the lives of those we have helped. We will also interview doctors who we have educated and sent overseas and who are now back and saving lives here! This isn't going to be about ribbon cutting but rather about showing and not telling our audience the difference its made.
metadata.Summary: A Brief History In the decade since the launch of the Carte Blanche ‘Making a Difference’ campaign, over R145-million has been raised to equip and renovate Paediatric Operating Theatres, ICUs and High Care Wards in 10 State academic hospitals in six of South Africa’s nine provinces. Each of the Trust’s projects have had the benefited from the expertise of some of the country’s top specialists in the fields of hospital development, architecture and clinical, electrical and mechanical engineering. Thousands of hours have been contributed for the benefit of each project’s success. In turn, this has resulted in long-term benefits to thousands of children in State hospitals throughout South Africa. The Carte Blanche “Making a Difference” Trust has commenced its 19th project, namely to create a new Paediatric Unit at Ngwelezana Hospital in KZN’s Umhlathuze Municipality. The upliftment of paediatric services for trauma, burns and orthopedic at the hospital will be addressed by way of overhauling a building that has been earmarked for this purpose and equipping it with appropriate equipment. In addition to the work in various hospitals, the trust has completed several projects in aftercare centres and orphanages, as well as initiating and securing the funding for feeding programmes for our child welfare beneficiaries in Gauteng, the North West province and KwaZulu-Natal.

What are the details of the new project, under construction - the Paeds Lower High Care Unit that, in his view, have significance on his and his teams wherewithal to deliver class care to the young of Sebokeng? How does this impact on him personally as a doctor? How did he provide personal input into planning & design of the new Unit? Has this been implemented practically? Acting Unit Manager: Nursing Sister Matieho Namani: Interview at 11H15 Similar questions as those posed to Dr Theletsane Dr Mashele: Sebokeng Hospital Clinical Manager: 11H30 How long has Dr worked at the Hospital? Dr Mashele is a closely involved member of team on building projects at the hospital – what is his view of the developments of Phase 1 & 2 and what bearing does this have on his Clinical Management of the hospital? What bearing do these projects have on the delivery of healthcare to the children of the Sedibeng community? Interviews: Billy Neethling: Jomarel Construction Principal and Foreman: Roland Marsh 11H45 July 2021 saw some of the worst acts of destruction and looting in decades in SA. This period intersected at the heart of the construction programme of our Paediatric Lower High Care Unit Project at Sebokeng Hospital. Thanks to the commitment of our contractors and local business owners and labourers, only one day of construction time was lost. From the community (remembering that these local companies employ a lot of locals who built the project) Sejako: Local lady business owner of ISS Plumbing: (plumbing on the project) 12H00 John: Local business owner of ATL Lupula Electrical (electricians for the project) 12H15 Jacob and John: local previously unemployed workmen from Sebokeng who worked on construction from start to end of project Background: The creation and equipping of the 6 bed Infant High Care Ward at Sebokeng Hospital, sponsored by South 32, has reference. In a period calculated as 21 months between September 2016 to May 2018: 348 infants have been assisted. The High Care Unit now attends to approximately 20 Infants per month each of whom has an average stay of roughly 3 days. Approximately 1/3 of the Ward 3 bungalow was used to create the High Care Ward, with the balance of 2/3rds of the space lying disconnected from services and unutilised. Sebokeng Hospital is a peri urban regional, level 2 hospital. Referrals arise from all the primary health care facilities in the Vaal from as well as from various Level 1 district hospitals including Kopanong. Sebokeng Hospital is servicing a burgeoning population of both formal and informal settlements in the Sedibeng District. The increased population and growth in burden of disease leaves Sebokeng in a position where it faces a shortage of bed capacity and critical infrastructural resources in meeting the needs of its community. As part of the endemic shortage of nurses and doctors in South Africa, Sebokeng Hospital also faces these critical staff shortages. The issue has been addressed with regards to doctors in the Infant High Care Ward, by way of agreements reached with Chris Hani Bara which sends two paediatric registrars to staff the NICU & Infant HCW. These positions are sponsored by Sebokeng Hospital which makes this training programme possible. Statement of need: All patients who arrive at Sebokeng Hospital are admitted via the Casualty Unit at the hospital – irrespective whether or not these patients be recently discharged neonates and children – or adults.The waiting time for babies is no different to adults and infants are assessed by people who are used to adults.The Nurses are operating at 25% of what is needed in terms of patient numbers and are not specialised in Neonatology or Paediatrics. There is capacity for 36 Neonates in the NICU, but even with the Infant High Care Ward in place, the NICU typically holds 42 – 56 neonates at any time. Infants should never ever be readmitted to the NICU, but diverted immediately to an Infant Facility in order to effect adequate infection control. Oftentimes there is only 1 ICU nurse to 6- 7 patients. This critical nurse shortage has impact on outcomes. Mortality of infants and children has actually increased in the General Casualty Admissions Ward. Due to the constraints of bed space, older children are also being admitted to the Infant High Care Unit – placing an additional restraint of capacity on these services. The Carte Blanche Making a Difference Trust seeks to address growing mortality by proposing to renovate the balance of 2/3rds of Ward 3 alongside the Infant High Care Unit. The greatest need is to create expanded neonatal & Infant High Care Capacity for children who are readmitted to the Hospital, and who should be quarantined. Apart from repairs need to the entire Ward 3 Bungalow roof including new sheeting and sealing, the 1st step would be to get medical gases and oxygen services back into the middle section of Ward 3, adjacent to the Infant High Care Ward. If left to the DOH, they would only replace pipes and points – not pendants to bring in the necessary services, nor extraction. In addition, The Carte Blanche Trust seeks to refurbish the 1st part of the Ward 3 bungalow into a dedicated Neonatal & Paediatric Casualty Admissions Ward. This would ensure that children are admitted/readmitted and diverted to the appropriate ward within a timeframe that prevents their deterioration, making them ineligible for treatment. Babies that are readmitted to Sebokeng Hospital would be separated permanently from their younger, more vulnerable peers. The Dedicated Neonatal & Casualty Ward should ideally cater for a walk in triage point centre with seating available, and 7 beds with 1 isolated overnight room (if contagions are suspected) in the back.
